name: Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans
title: Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans
answer: Synthetic imaging from existing scans is the practice of generating new medical images, or new contrast or modality views, from one or more already acquired scans. It includes cross-modality translation such as synthetic CT from MRI, virtual contrast enhancement, super-resolution, and removal of artifacts or metal. The goal is to reduce repeat scanning, lower radiation or contrast exposure, and fill gaps where a desired sequence was not obtained. In radiology, these outputs are used for treatment planning, diagnostic review, and training or validation of other imaging models.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Synthetic imaging from existing scans is the practice of generating new medical images, or new contrast or modality views, from one or more already acquired scans. It includes cross-modality translation such as synthetic CT from MRI, virtual contrast enhancement, super-resolution, and removal of artifacts or metal. The goal is to reduce repeat scanning, lower radiation or contrast exposure, and fill gaps where a desired sequence was not obtained. In radiology, these outputs are used for treatment planning, diagnostic review, and training or validation of other imaging models.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard hospital imaging archives and GPU servers, often integrated with PACS and radiology workflow systems. Models are typically trained on paired or unpaired scan datasets and deployed as inference services that receive DICOM studies and return derived DICOM series. Because synthetic images can be large, deployment usually requires high-throughput storage, fast network access to scanners, and versioned model containers. Many sites run these models on institutional hardware or through regulated cloud environments rather than on the scanner itself.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Most approaches use deep convolutional networks, generative adversarial networks, diffusion models, or vision transformers trained to map one image domain to another. Training may be supervised with aligned pairs, such as the same patient scanned with and without contrast, or unsupervised with cycle consistency across unpaired sets. Radiologists and physicists typically validate outputs by comparing synthetic images against real acquisitions using quantitative metrics like structural similarity, peak signal-to-noise ratio, and downstream task performance. The work is done by multidisciplinary teams that include radiologists, medical physicists, and machine learning engineers, with careful review of failure modes such as hallucinated lesions or altered texture.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Synthetic images raise questions about provenance, because a generated scan can look like an acquired one and may be mistaken for ground truth. Rights and risk center on patient consent for secondary use of scans, data protection, and liability when a synthetic image contributes to a missed or false finding. The site tracks six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows that harm claims can reach synthetic imaging tools if they are used clinically. Compliance pages and model cards increasingly require clear labeling of synthetic series, audit trails, and disclosure of training data provenance. Institutions generally treat synthetic images as derived data subject to the same privacy and retention rules as the source scans.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward routine synthetic contrast and cross-modality translation that reduce patient burden and scanner time. Future work will likely focus on prospective clinical trials, standardized quality assurance, and real-time generation during scanning to complete missing sequences. As models become more common, regulators and radiology societies are expected to define when a synthetic image may substitute for an acquired one and when it must be flagged. The atlas tracks this shift across its collection of medical AI models and compliance pages, reflecting a gradual move from research demonstrations to governed clinical use.
